Through the years, owning shares of Microsoft has made many investors rich—and turned company executives into billionaires. But Microsoft's richest individual shareholders aren't necessarily who you might think. Although he's vowed to give most of his fortune away, Bill Gates, Microsoft's co-founder and longtime CEO, still owns approximately $55 billion worth of MSFT shares as of October 2026. And the company's current CEO, Satya Nadella, has an ownership stake valued around just around $489 million. But there's another Microsoft leader who owns considerably more stock than either Gates or Nadella—that's Steve Ballmer, who ran the company from 2000 to 2014. In fact, Ballmer is Microsoft's largest individual shareholder, with an estimated stake worth around $170 billion. Because Ballmer is no longer a Microsoft executive or a member of its board of directors, and his holdings are below the 5% disclosure threshold required by the SEC, it is difficult to tell exactly how many shares of MSFT the former CEO still owns. We can, however, follow his paper trail of news reports and SEC filings, starting with Ballmer's SEC Form 4 filed after he stepped down from the company in 2014. In this disclosure, Ballmer reported that he owned 333,254,734 shares of MSFT. Ballmer also appears in Bloomberg's Billionaires Index, which estimates that he had sold approximately 14 million shares to help finance his $2 billion purchase of the Los Angeles Clippers in 2014. Subtract 14 million and we get approximately 319 million MSFT shares held, which the consensus estimate of Ballmer's current holdings. In 2024, Ballmer told The Wall Street Journal  that "The only stock I really study still is Microsoft, because that's still overwhelmingly, overwhelmingly, overwhelmingly the No. 1 thing that I own." In 2025, Ballmer spoke with GeekWire, which reported that he remained Microsoft's largest individual shareholder. And while Ballmer has also made sizable charitable donations and grants through the Ballmer Group, Bloomberg notes that it had deducted more than $2 billion from his estimated cash holdings to account for charitable giving. Assuming Ballmer continues to hold roughly 319 million shares of Microsoft in 2026, and  using MSFT's October 21, 2026 closing price of $532.95, that would put the value of his stake at approximately $170 billion, or around 4.3% of outstanding shares. Under Ballmer, Microsoft's annual revenue grew from $25 billion to nearly $80 billion, and its net income soared over 200%. He helped to spearhead the company's foray into the Cloud, oversaw the acquisition of Skype, and launched the Xbox gaming system and Bing search engine. But Ballmer also made some epic missteps, including misunderstanding the importance of open-source technology, overseeing a disastrous launch of Windows 8, and actually laughing at the Apple iPhone when it was introduced in 2007, saying, "there's no chance that the iPhone is going to get any significant market share." Ballmer's last major acquisition as CEO came in 2013, when Microsoft agreed to purchase Nokia's mobile phone business. The deal resulted in billions in write-downs and thousands of layoffs, and Ballmer stepped down as CEO ins February 2014. He left Microsoft's board of directors later that year. So, how did he acquire such a large stake in Microsoft? To answer that, we must go back in time—way back, to 1980. Ballmer was Microsoft's 30th employee and its first business manager. He had previously lived down the hall from Bill Gates at Harvard, and while Ballmer was pursuing his MBA at Stanford, Gates offered him a job to help manage his business. Ballmer's base salary was $50,000 plus 10% of the company's profit growth. As the business took off, Microsoft reorganized into a corporation in 1981, and Ballmer agreed to trade his profit-sharing for an 8% ownership stake. Microsoft's other co-founder, Paul Allen, initially objected to Ballmer receiving such a large stake. But Gates agreed to give up a portion of his own ownership to make things work out. In 2003, in order to diversify his portfolio, Ballmer sold 39.3 million MSFT shares for approximately $955 million. This reduced his ownership stake down to around 4%. Even though Ballmer is estimated to hold roughly 4% of MSFT's outstanding shares in 2026, institutional investors have an even greater stake in the tech giant. According to Microsoft's latest Proxy Statement, Vanguard Capital Management holds 555,988,240 shares, or 7.48% of Microsoft. As of MSFT's October 21 close, Vanguard's stake is worth $296.3 billion, and BlackRock's approximately $287.8 billion. Together, they own $584.1 billion of Microsoft stock. title: MSFT Stock Rises Premarket Ahead Of Q4 Results: CapEx, Azure Growth In Focus - Stocktwits
content: Microsoft rose 1% in early premarket trading on Wednesday, ahead of its quarterly report after the markets close. Once one of the key stocks rising in the AI wave, Microsoft has lost its crown as investors’ focus has turned to its heavy spending and increasing competition from AI and cloud rivals. Microsoft has forecast spending $190 billion in capital expenditures in calendar year 2026. The spending trend in the fiscal fourth quarter, which ended in June, as well as any changes to its full-year guidance, would be closely watched. Alphabet’s move makes it more likely that Amazon and Microsoft will follow suit, according to Evercore ISI. Alphabet’s capex boost “increases the odds of similar behavior” from Amazon and Microsoft, analyst Mark Mahaney said in a recent investor note. Shares of Amazon, Meta and Microsoft tumbled last week after Alphabet’s CapEx forecast hike, even as the search company reported accelerating cloud growth. The growth in Amazon’s cloud unit, Azure, would also be key, with Google setting a high bar. Google Cloud sales increased a record 82% last quarter. Revenue from Microsoft’s Azure and other cloud services grew 40% in the company’s fiscal third quarter. Investors will also closely track subscription growth for Microsoft’s flagship AI product, Microsoft 365 Copilot, which has seen tepid adoption. Although shares have risen in July, it has been a difficult stretch for Microsoft in the stock market. MSFT shares fell 23% in the first six months of the year, marking their worst half-year performance since 2000 and the weakest showing among the Magnificent Seven stocks in the first half of 2026. MSFT is down 18.3% year-to-date. Microsoft has come under pressure amid a broader selloff in software stocks, hefty capital spending plans and intensifying competition in AI from Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI. Earlier this month, Microsoft carried out a major restructuring at its Xbox division, cutting some 3,200 jobs. The company also said at the time that it would sell or spin off five game development studios. In June, Microsoft eliminated 6,000 roles, or about 4% of its workforce, primarily across product and engineering teams. Analysts expect Microsoft’s fiscal fourth quarter revenue to rise 15% to $87.63 billion – which would be the lowest in the last five quarters – and adjusted profit to also increase by the same degree to $4.22 per share, per Koyfin data. Currently, 50 out of 53 analysts rate MSFT stock ‘Buy’ or higher and the remaining three rate it ‘Hold,’ per Koyfin data. Their average price target of $555.77 implies a 41% upside from the stock’s closing price on Tuesday. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment for MSFT was ‘neutral,’ unchanged for the past two weeks. “$MSFT this has taken a nosedive too many times after earnings. I think PT's will be on track after tomorrow. 550 years end,” a trader wrote, forecasting the stock to run 40% higher. To be sure, the Federal Reserve’s interest rate decision on Wednesday afternoon will also likely influence Microsoft stock and the broader market. Shares of Tesla, Inc. (TSLA) and SpaceX (SPCX) slipped in overnight trading heading into Wednesday, but RBC Capital sees a potential combination of Elon Musk’s two companies creating an “orbit-to-ground” platform with more than $1 trillion in long-term chip savings. SPCX stock is down about 2% in overnight trading heading into Wednesday, while TSLA shares are off more than 1%. SpaceX snapped a two-session losing streak with a 3% gain on Tuesday, while Tesla extended its decline to a fifth consecutive session. RBC Capital lowered its Tesla price target to $480 from $500, implying a 56% upside from current levels, while maintaining an ‘Outperform’ rating. The brokerage said that a potential Tesla-SpaceX merger could create a compelling “vertical integration from orbit to ground” ecosystem spanning connectivity, autonomous vehicles and humanoid robotics that would be difficult to replicate. RBC sees Terafab, Musk’s vertically integrated semiconductor manufacturing complex for AI chips used across Tesla and SpaceX, as the most tangible near-term synergy, estimating it could generate well over $1 trillion in chip-cost savings by 2050 compared with relying on external suppliers. Earlier this month, UBS estimated SpaceX could spend about $135 billion on wafer-fabrication equipment over the next five years, assuming 20% of its projected $1.1 trillion capital-spending program goes toward Terafab. Musk said in Tesla’s latest earnings call that there was “more and more overlap” with SpaceX and singled out Terafab as a “gigantic project.” Tesla General Counsel Brandon Ehrhart said the companies had deepened their relationship earlier this year through an investment and framework agreement covering projects including Terafab and Digital Optimus. However, Musk declined to discuss a combination directly, saying any such transaction would have to follow the appropriate process. But, the overlap already extends well beyond chips. Musk said Starlink is being integrated into Cybercab and is expected to reach Tesla vehicles in markets where the satellite service operates, arguing reliable connectivity is essential for Robotaxis that cannot afford coverage gaps. Tesla is also working with SpaceX on Digital Optimus, with Grok serving as a higher-level model that assigns tasks to the system. Tesla is developing Megapod compute systems that pair its AI hardware with conventional processors and can be deployed near available power infrastructure. Musk said Terafab is “necessary” to scale Optimus because Tesla otherwise risks running short of AI chips, adding that the project will need to address memory, logic and packaging. The company has already placed equipment orders for an Austin development fab designed to combine mask production, logic, memory, packaging and testing under one roof. Tesla is also advancing its AI5 and AI6 chips, with AI5 expected to initially go into Optimus. Shares of ImmunityBio, Inc. (IBRX) are extending a five-session losing streak, but retail traders are looking to next week’s earnings for signs that “incredibly strong” Anktiva sales can reverse the slide. IBRX stock slipped 0.3% on Tuesday, with shares on track to log their fourth straight week in the red. The focus is on commercial momentum for Anktiva, ImmunityBio’s flagship immunotherapy, after CEO Richard Adcock apparently struck an upbeat tone at a BTIG virtual conference ahead of the company’s expected quarterly report next week.  According to a trader following Adcock’s BTIG appearance, the CEO said sales were continuing “at the same pace” and later described them as “incredibly strong.” Koyfin estimates call for quarterly revenue of $49.7 million, up 12% from the prior quarter. Profitability is also expected to improve, with GAAP loss per share narrowing to $0.09 from $0.62, while adjusted loss per share is expected to remain at $0.08. Retail expectations are running hotter than consensus, with traders dissecting comments from the company, treatment volumes and international sales ahead of the second-quarter (Q2) print. However, retail sentiment on Stocktwits for IBRX was ‘bearish’ amid an 18% rise in 24-hour message volumes. One investor expects about $51 million in quarterly revenue, while another cited a Street estimate around $49 million and a “whisper” range of $52 million to $54 million. Others have floated even more aggressive numbers, including $60 million to $63 million in Q2 sales. One trader said repeat dosing of existing patients could produce a much stronger quarter than expected, saying the “potential for a huge quarter does exist” and that “EVERYONE has Underestimated the Potential.” Another trader said: “Earnings beat will stop the bleeding.” Retail investors are also watching for partnership or buyout developments. Some have speculated that a larger pharma company could help ImmunityBio accelerate global distribution, while others continue to view the company as a potential acquisition candidate if Anktiva sales keep expanding. Beyond the quarter, ImmunityBio is building a broader strategy around Anktiva and its natural killer, or NK, cell platform. Founder Patrick Soon-Shiong has outlined plans for a global “World Bank of NK Cells,” to create a scalable supply of cryopreserved, off-the-shelf NK cells that could be distributed to patients and deployed alongside Anktiva. The company is also developing automated manufacturing through its Nant Leonardo robotic platform. Soon-Shiong said in June that the NK-cell bank would ultimately be made available globally. Anktiva itself has also been expanding beyond the U.S., with ImmunityBio pursuing commercial and regulatory opportunities across Europe, Saudi Arabia and other markets. ImmunityBio also has a regulatory catalyst beyond the immediate earnings print. In May, the Food and Drug Administration accepted the company’s application seeking to expand Anktiva plus BCG into a broader group of patients with BCG-unresponsive non-muscle invasive bladder cancer, reversing an earlier refusal to review a similar filing. The agency set Jan. 6, 2027, as the target date for its decision. ImmunityBio has said its Quilt-3.032 study showed 58% of high-risk papillary bladder cancer patients remained disease-free at 12 months, while more than 80% avoided bladder-removal surgery through three years of follow-up. Corning reported earnings per share (EPS) of $0.78 on revenue of $4.74 billion, beating Wall Street estimates of an EPS of $0.75 on revenue of $4.63 billion, according to Fiscal.ai data. Corning shares were down more than 16% in Tuesday’s pre-market trade. GLW was among the top trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing. Corning’s third-quarter (Q3) guidance fell short of Wall Street expectations, with the company’s softer near-term outlook weighing on the stock ahead of the opening bell on Tuesday. The specialty glass and materials maker forecast EPS between $0.85 and $0.89. At a midpoint of $0.87, Corning’s Q3 EPS forecast is slightly ahead of a consensus estimate of $0.85. Corning also expects its Q3 revenue to come in between $4.9 billion and $5 billion. At a midpoint of $4.95 billion, it misses the consensus estimate of $5 billion. Corning’s solar and life sciences segments swung to a quarterly loss in Q2. The company reported a net loss of $7 million in the solar segment, compared to a profit of $2 million during the year-ago period. However, the solar segment’s revenue surged 90% year-on-year to $438 million. The life sciences segment performed relatively worse, with a net loss of $21 million compared to a profit of $6 million during the same period a year ago. Revenue declined 15% YoY to $294 million. Corning stated that it completed an extended maintenance shutdown and equipment upgrade at its solar wafer facility during the quarter. It also expects profitability to improve during Q3. “We also expect an improving impact on earnings from Solar starting in Q3 as our ramp continues, building toward a revenue stream of more than $3 billion with strong profit and cash flow,” said Corning CFO Ed Schlesinger. Corning CEO Wendell Weeks said that the company is entering a “new phase of accelerating growth” after delivering what he described as an outstanding second quarter. The company upgraded its Springboard Plan and now expects to reach an annualized sales run rate of $20 billion by the end of 2026, $30 billion by the end of 2028, and $40 billion by the end of 2030. Weeks added that Corning expects to deliver a 19% compound annual growth rate in sales from the fourth quarter (Q4) of 2026 through Q4 of 2030. Weeks said these partnerships provide “strong proof points” supporting the company's Springboard growth plan. Shares of Altimmune (ALT) jumped more than 10% in pre-market trading on Tuesday, after it reported positive topline results for its therapy to treat patients with moderate to severe alcohol use disorder (AUD), a condition with significant unmet medical need and limited treatment options. If the pre-market levels hold through the day, ALT stock would record its biggest single-day gains since Jan. 22, 2026. Data from Altimmune’s Phase 2 RECLAIM trial showed that Pemvidutide achieved positive topline results. The once-weekly 2.4 mg dose significantly reduced heavy drinking days, the trial’s primary endpoint, compared with placebo. The study enrolled about 100 patients who received either Pemvidutide or placebo for 24 weeks, with the drug showing a statistically significant reduction in heavy drinking days. Patients treated with Pemvidutide reduced heavy drinking by 4.20 days per week compared with the placebo’s 2.75 days and saw a substantially higher rate of meaningful reductions in drinking risk. In the final month of treatment, 42% of Pemvidutide patients had no heavy drinking days compared with 17% on placebo, while alcohol-free days increased by 38.9% versus 20.5% with placebo. Pemvidutide also produced a placebo-adjusted weight reduction of 9.1% at 24 weeks. AUD is a serious condition in which people struggle to stop or control harmful alcohol use, affecting an estimated 28 million adults in the U.S. It increases the risk of serious health problems such as liver disease, heart disease, cancer, obesity, and fatty liver. The topline results are important because they showed consistent improvements across several measures of alcohol use disorder, which objectively reflect lower alcohol consumption. The findings suggest Pemvidutide could potentially address multiple aspects of the disease while also building on earlier evidence of liver-related benefits. “These top-line data strengthen our confidence in Pemvidutide’s differentiation and its potential to benefit people living with MASH, AUD and ALD, who currently have limited treatment options,” said Jerry Durso, Chief Executive Officer and Chairman of the Board of Altimmune. title: US Tech Stocks Under Pressure: 3 Stocks to Watch Before Next Week’s Earnings - TradingView
content: US tech stocks are entering a pivotal earnings week as investors question whether the AI boom can justify its mounting costs. The Nasdaq Composite fell 0.21% on October 23 to close at 25,955.34, while the S&P 500 dropped 0.52% to 7,623.68, extending its weekly decline. With Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon preparing to report results, investors will scrutinize cloud growth, AI monetization, and capital expenditure for signs that heavy investments are translating into sustainable earnings. The upcoming reports could test whether the recent pullback is a temporary setback or a broader reassessment of AI valuations. 1. Microsoft (MSFT) Stock: Can Azure Growth Ease AI Spending Concerns? Microsoft reports its fiscal first-quarter 2027 results on October 28, with Wall Street focused on Azure growth, Copilot adoption, and AI infrastructure spending. Analysts expect earnings of $4.71 per share on revenue of $90.63 billion. The key question is whether accelerating AI demand can support Microsoft’s growth without putting further pressure on margins and cash flow. Investors will also assess management’s outlook for Azure and future capital expenditure. Strong cloud guidance and evidence of AI monetization could restore confidence. Slower growth or higher-than-expected spending could intensify concerns about investment returns. 2. Alphabet (GOOGL) Stock: Can Google Cloud Strengthen the Earnings Outlook? Alphabet reports earnings on October 28 as investors assess Google Cloud growth, advertising demand, and the financial impact of AI-powered search. Analysts expect earnings of $3.03 per share on revenue of approximately $127.92 billion. Google Cloud’s performance will be particularly important as Alphabet expands its AI infrastructure. Meanwhile, investors will look for evidence that AI-powered search can preserve advertising growth while creating new monetization opportunities. Strong cloud results and resilient advertising revenue could support the stock. Rising investment costs combined with weaker search growth could leave investors questioning the returns from Alphabet’s AI strategy. 3. Amazon (AMZN) Stock: Will AWS Growth Offset Rising AI Costs? Amazon is scheduled to report earnings on October 29, putting AWS revenue growth, operating margins, and AI infrastructure spending in focus. Analysts expect earnings of $1.96 per share on revenue of approximately $202 billion. AWS remains central to Amazon’s profitability and AI strategy. Investors will assess whether demand for cloud computing and AI services can sustain growth while the company expands its infrastructure. Retail margins and forward guidance will also influence expectations for overall profitability. Strong AWS growth and improving margins could support the bullish case. Higher spending without a corresponding improvement in revenue expectations could weigh on investor confidence. Big Tech Earnings Could Set the Market’s Next Direction Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon face a common challenge: demonstrating that AI investments can generate sustainable financial returns. Azure, Google Cloud, and AWS growth will offer important clues, but capital expenditure and forward guidance could ultimately determine how investors respond. If cloud growth and AI monetization exceed expectations, the results could help stabilize US tech stocks. If spending rises faster than returns, the sector’s valuation concerns may persist. title: Microsoft's Earnings Problem: Even Great May Not Be Enough - The Globe and Mail
content: Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ: MSFT) heads into its Q1 report for fiscal year 2027 (FY2027) with very little room for error. The stock closed at over $530 per share on Oct. 21; that's within striking distance of its 52-week high of $553.72. MSFT is up about 33% since the company last reported earnings, raising the stakes for this release, scheduled after the market closes on Wednesday, Oct. 28. A stock near its high has already priced in plenty of good news. That's why a clean beat may not be enough to push it higher. Investors will want a beat that also raises the bar for the rest of the fiscal year. The good news is that analysts don't appear to be worried. The Microsoft analyst forecasts on MarketBeat give the stock a consensus price target of $592.15, up from $578.73 less than two weeks ago. That implies roughly 12% upside from current levels. Adding to the bullish sentiment, of the 49 analysts MarketBeat tracks, 43 rate the stock a Buy. The latest moves are notable. Jefferies raised its target from $575 to $650 on Oct. 14. Citigroup followed a day later, lifting its target from $600 to $636. Wells Fargo sits near the high end of the range with a $725 target. As usual, Azure is the headline number to watch. Last quarter, Azure grew 43%, ahead of the 40% analysts expected. The business also topped $100 billion in annual revenue for the first time. Then management raised the stakes. Microsoft guided for 45% Azure growth in constant currency this quarter. That was well above the roughly 41% analysts had modeled at the time. However, that makes 45% the baseline, not the upside case. The market has a history of punishing Microsoft for small misses. In January, Azure grew 38%, beating guidance. The stock still fell 10% because the buy side was expecting more. Microsoft guided for total revenue between $89.85 billion and $90.95 billion. Analysts expect earnings of roughly $4.70 per share. Last quarter, the company posted $4.74 per share, topping the consensus by 50 cents. The second number may matter even more. Microsoft guided for about $50 billion in capital expenditure (CapEx) this quarter. That's up from roughly $36 billion in the prior quarter. The company also projected $175 billion in CapEx for calendar 2026. Investors will listen closely to the tone around that spending. Microsoft has said demand still exceeds its available capacity. That's the bullish case for continued investment. But any hint of a pause would ripple far beyond Redmond. Chipmakers, data center operators and power suppliers all depend on hyperscaler budgets. A slowdown signal from Microsoft would likely be read as a bearish sign for the broader AI trade. There's a counterweight to watch. Free cash flow fell 23% year over year last quarter. Investors want spending to stay aggressive, but they also want proof it's paying off. Gaming rarely moves Microsoft stock, but it could shape the narrative. In July, CEO Satya Nadella said he expects Xbox to return to growth in fiscal 2027. That's a bold promise after a rough year. Xbox revenue fell 7% in fiscal 2026. Hardware revenue dropped 29% on lower console sales. Content and services, which include Game Pass, declined 10% in the fourth quarter alone. Management guided for another mid-single-digit decline this quarter. That makes October's launch of Gears of War: E-Day an early test. The game set a franchise record with more than 31,000 concurrent players on Steam. Yet estimates from Alinea Analytics put early unit sales at only about 230,000 copies. The bigger number is subscriptions. The same estimates show about 1.7 million players accessing the game through Game Pass. Microsoft is betting on recurring subscription revenue over one-time game sales. Gears launched in the current quarter, so it won't show up in these results. But management's holiday-quarter outlook could reveal how much it's counting on the franchise. Any update on Game Pass growth will be a tell for the turnaround. The technical picture is constructive, but momentum is fading. MSFT gapped higher after its July report and has trended up since. The stock remains well above its rising 50-day simple moving average (SMA), now near $507. However, the stock stalled near $550 in mid-October. That's close to where it peaked last fall before a long decline. A failure to clear that level would raise the risk of a double top. The MACD indicator adds to the caution. The MACD line has crossed below its signal line, and the histogram has turned negative. MACD also made a lower high in October, even as the stock made a higher high. That bearish divergence suggests buyers are losing conviction. Initial support sits near $515, the top of the August-September trading range. Below that, the 50-day SMA near $507 is the next key level. On the upside, a decisive close above $554 would confirm the breakout. Before you make your next trade, you'll want to hear this. title: Microsoft Has a $1 Trillion Opportunity Hiding in Plain Sight - 24/7 Wall St.
content: Azure just crossed a milestone that has analysts quietly raising their ceiling for Microsoft, but the real story is buried in a contract number that almost nobody is talking about. Our 24/7 Wall St. price target for Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction) is $647.87 over the next 12 months. From a current price of $531.90, that implies 21.8% upside. Our model rates the stock a buy, and we hold that view with high confidence. The opportunity hiding in plain sight is contracted demand. Commercial remaining performance obligations rose 84% to $678 billion, and the portion recognized beyond 12 months jumped 112%. Azure exceeded $100 billion in annual revenue, and the CFO said demand “continues to exceed available capacity.” That backlog is the path toward a trillion-dollar cloud and AI franchise. Microsoft slipped 2.19% over the past week but gained 7.65% over the past month and 10.61% year to date. It sits about 3.5% below its 52-week high of $551.15 and roughly 52.6% above its low of $348.54. Fiscal Q4 revenue of $90.01 billion beat the $87.63 billion consensus, and EPS of $4.74 exceeded the $4.2394 estimate. That was the fifth consecutive EPS beat. Azure grew 43%, and management forecast for about 45% in constant currency this quarter. Away from the fundamentals, Microsoft also joined other blue chips this week in pushing back against efforts to tokenize their stocks. Our bull scenario reaches $752.32, a 41.44% gain. Microsoft 365 Copilot has passed 30 million paid seats, and net seat adds more than doubled quarter over quarter. Pricing is moving to seat plus usage, which CEO Satya Nadella said makes “the TAM much more expansive.” GitHub Copilot has reached 50 million users, and Microsoft expects to roughly double its total capacity in two years. Analysts agree: 14 rate the stock Strong Buy, 39 give a Buy rating, and none rate it Sell. Their consensus target is $599.28. Fiscal 2026 capex rose 79.62% to $115.95 billion, while free cash flow fell 6.46%. Microsoft Cloud gross margin slipped to 65%, and Xbox revenue fell 10%. If the worst-case scenario plays out, shares reach just $547.61. One fair counterpoint is that about two-thirds of capex goes to short-lived CPUs and GPUs, the same supplier network we broke down in a free report on seven companies powering the AI buildout beyond the chipmakers. The CFO said that “if the demand environment changes, you just slow down” that spending. Microsoft also expects to stay free-cash-flow positive in fiscal 2027. Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) is the most direct rival in AI infrastructure. Its low P/E is inflated by a $99.03 billion gain on equity securities, and its free cash flow turned negative at -$5.86 billion. Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) runs AWS, which grew 37%, yet the stock trades at a higher P/E than Microsoft. Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) has a similar backlog of $664 billion but posted negative free cash flow of -$5.40 billion. Measured against these peers, the 24/7 Wall St. price target looks reasonable, even modest. Our 24/7 Wall St. price target of $647.87 carries a buy rating with 90% confidence. What tips the scale is a growing contracted backlog coupled with positive free cash flow. The case improves if Azure delivers the forecast acceleration and Copilot usage revenue scales. I’d be more cautious if capex keeps rising while Azure growth stalls. For now, I think the backlog more than supports the spending. These estimates rely on Microsoft continuing to carry out its current AI strategy. title: Could You Have Seen The Run In Microsoft Stock Coming? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Microsoft (MSFT) stock returned 36.8% from July 24 to October 22, 2026, against 3.7% for the S&P 500. This rally followed a period where the shares had lost 17.7% over the six months before July 24. By the end of this run, investors were paying a much higher price for the same twelve months of Microsoft’s earnings. What had Microsoft told investors before July 24? Well over a year before the run, management told investors that customers were buying more. On its January 29, 2025 call, management said large companies were beginning to move from small trials to “enterprise-wide deployments”, and that commercial bookings, the contracts customers sign for future sales, had increased 67%, a jump the finance chief said was driven by Azure commitments from OpenAI. Six months later, on the July 30, 2025 call, management said Azure, its cloud platform, had passed $75 billion in annual revenue, up 34%. This expansion was more than twice the 14.9% growth Microsoft reported as a whole for fiscal 2025. Company filings reinforced these statements. Microsoft’s revenue growth from a year earlier rose from 13.3% in the quarter ended March 2025 to 18.1% in the quarter ended June 2025. Growth was still 18.3% in the quarter ended March 2026, which Microsoft filed on April 29, 2026, before the run. The evidence was public and held steady, but the shares still lost 17.7% in the six months before July 24. How Much More Investors Now Pay For Microsoft’s Earnings At the October 22 close, investors paid 28.9 times Microsoft’s earnings for the twelve months to June 2026, against 20.7 times at the end of June. The end-of-June multiple was the lowest at any quarter end since fiscal 2017. The business maintained the pace shown in its earlier filings. In the quarter ended June 2026, Microsoft’s revenue was $90.0 billion, up 17.7% from a year earlier. The shares rose 15.5% on July 30, 2026, marking the biggest one-day move of the run. Microsoft’s performance diverged notably from its mega-cap peers over this three-month span. Alphabet, Amazon and Apple stock each returned 7.9% or less over the same three months. On sales, yes. Microsoft’s revenue grew between 16.7% and 18.4% from a year earlier in each of the four quarters to June 2026, much the same pace the filings showed before the run. Profit on each dollar of those sales has slipped, however. Microsoft’s operating margin fell in each of the last three quarters, dropping from 48.9% in the quarter ended September 2025 to 45.1% in the quarter ended June 2026. This figure remained above the 44.9% of a year earlier. Over the full twelve months, the margin was still 46.8%, against 18.5% for the S&P 500 taken as one company. Microsoft is expected to report next on October 28, 2026, and its revenue growth from a year earlier is the number to watch. Your Advisor Retired? We came across a bullish thesis on Alphabet Inc. on Astute Optics - US's Substack. In this article, we will summarize the bulls' thesis on GOOGL. Alphabet Inc.'s share was trading at $334.76 as of October 21st 2026. GOOGL's trailing and forward P/E were 17.62 and 22.83 respectively according to Yahoo Finance. This isn't the first time we see a technology company pitched as a great investment. GOOGL shares gained 35.20% over the last 12 months. Comparable stocks like Amazon gained 20.50% during the same period. Strong gains can attract investors, but GOOGL's recent pullback raises a different question: has the weakness created a buying opportunity, or is there more reason for caution? In July, we published an article about the 10 Best Quantum Computing Stocks to Buy and Hold Forever and GOOGL ranked #3 in that article. While GOOGL has edged slightly lower since then, the #1 stock in that list returned 41.18% over the same period. So, hedge funds were right about their #1 pick while GOOGL's performance has been more subdued. This article explains why hedge funds were bullish on GOOGL. Before getting into our analysis, let's take a look at the business and why some investors like the stock so much. Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) provides internet services and technology platforms through Google Services, Google Cloud, and Other Bets. Its core business still centers on Google Search, YouTube, Android, Chrome, Maps, and advertising, but the real question for investors is whether artificial intelligence and cloud computing can become its next big growth drivers. Over the past year, revenue reached $445.9 billion, up 20.1%, and profitability improved as well, with margins climbing to healthy levels. The stock trades below the industry average on a headline basis, which on the surface makes it look cheaper than peers — though once one-time gains are stripped out, the valuation looks closer to the sector average. In short, the market isn't just paying for what Alphabet Inc. earns today; it's betting on years of AI and cloud-driven growth ahead. Read More: 15 AI Stocks That Are Quietly Making Investors Rich Read More: Undervalued AI Stock Poised For Massive Gains: 10000% Upside Potential The bullish case is that Alphabet Inc. can use its massive existing user base to turn AI into real revenue across multiple businesses. Google Search keeps driving advertising income, while Google Cloud is emerging as a fast-growing enterprise business as companies adopt AI tools and Gemini-based products. Recent results back this up: quarterly revenue grew 24% year over year to $119.8 billion, and Google Cloud revenue jumped 82% to $24.8 billion as businesses ramped up spending on AI infrastructure. If that trend continues, bulls believe Alphabet Inc. can grow both from higher cloud demand and new ways to monetize AI across its platforms. The company is backing this optimism with money: it raised its capital spending plans to a range of $195 billion to $205 billion to build out data centers and AI capacity. It can afford to, given a net cash position of $144.3 billion and $164.7 billion in operating cash flow last fiscal year. That financial cushion means Alphabet Inc. can keep funding its AI buildout without straining its balance sheet, which supports the bull case that this could be a multi-year growth story rather than a single strong quarter. You can check out whether Amazon or Alphabet makes the stronger AI cloud investment case after the spending bill here. Wall Street largely shares that optimism. The average analyst price target of $422 implies roughly 26% upside from current levels, with estimates ranging widely depending on how much credit analysts give to AI and cloud growth. For that upside to materialize, though, Alphabet Inc. will need to keep converting its AI investments into actual earnings growth — if that monetization slows, these expectations could prove too optimistic. The biggest risk is that all this spending doesn't pay off fast enough. If AI is truly opening a new growth cycle, investors will expect the money being poured into infrastructure to eventually show up as stronger profits. Rising capital spending adds execution risk, and regulatory scrutiny over search and advertising practices could threaten some of Alphabet Inc.'s most profitable businesses. On top of that, newer AI-powered search tools are creating fresh uncertainty about the long-term strength of its core advertising model. Another risk for the stock is businesses cutting advertising budgets when economic conditions weaken. Google can retain its users and search traffic while advertisers spend less to reach them. Alphabet generated more than 70% of its revenue from online advertising in 2025, leaving it heavily exposed to those spending decisions. Weaker consumer demand could prompt advertisers to reduce campaigns or lower their bids. That would pressure advertising revenue even without Google losing market share to AI competitors. Cloud growth may not fully offset a slowdown across its much larger advertising business. In our opinion, this dependence could pressure Alphabet's price multiples if advertising weakens before newer businesses contribute enough profit. Hedge fund positioning shows a mixed signal. As per our database, 275 hedge funds held Alphabet Inc. at the end of the second quarter, up from 265 the quarter before — a modest increase suggesting institutional investors remain generally confident in its AI and cloud story despite valuation and regulatory concerns. By comparison, Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) was held by 273 hedge funds, down from 282, Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) was held by 369 hedge funds, up from 353, and Meta Platforms Inc. was held by 254 hedge funds, down from 262. Amazon.com Inc. clearly saw the strongest jump in institutional interest, while Alphabet Inc. gained ground compared with Microsoft Corporation and Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META), pointing to continued confidence in large-cap tech names tied to AI. Short interest data also paints a fairly calm picture. About 1.37% of Alphabet Inc.'s float is sold short, versus 0.82% for Microsoft Corporation, 0.88% for Amazon.com, Inc., and 1.52% for Meta Platforms, Inc. That's higher than Microsoft Corporation and Amazon.com, Inc. but slightly below Meta Platforms, Inc., suggesting some investors are watching Alphabet Inc.'s spending, valuation, and regulatory risks more closely than those of Microsoft Corporation and Amazon.com, Inc. Even so, short interest remains low across all four companies, suggesting limited outright bearish conviction across the group. GOOGL's forward P/E is 22.83x. Microsoft Corporation, Amazon.com, Inc., and Meta Platforms, Inc. trade at forward P/Es of 25.13x, 23.64x, and 22.08x, respectively. GOOGL's own forward P/E was 28.01x on December 31, 2025, meaning its current valuation is approximately 18% lower. We believe the current valuation reflects significant investor concerns about rising AI spending, competition in search, and regulatory pressure. However, its modest discounts to Microsoft and Amazon and slight premium to Meta suggest the stock is reasonably priced rather than deeply undervalued. Alphabet Inc.'s trailing revenue increased 20.1% to $445.9 billion, while second-quarter revenue grew approximately 24%, although large investment gains inflated reported profits and should not be treated as recurring earnings growth. We believe Alphabet can justify 22.83 times forward earnings if its advertising and cloud businesses sustain double-digit earnings growth after rising infrastructure costs, allowing shareholder returns without requiring a higher P/E. If Alphabet turns AI demand into lasting profits and maintains sufficient cash flow after capital spending, the current valuation could offer an attractive entry point despite its execution and regulatory risks. Not many people remember this, but when Satya Nadella took the reins as CEO of Microsoft in February 2014, the company was struggling to find its place amidst a tech landscape dominated by Apple's smartphones, Google's Android operating system, and Amazon's cloud computing services. Under the leadership of Steve Ballmer, Microsoft had undertaken a contentious $7.2 billion acquisition of Nokia's mobile phone business in 2013. That deal ultimately failed, resulting in billions in write-downs and thousands of layoffs. But Nadella did not turn the company around overnight. Over the next few years, he shifted Microsoft's business model even further into cloud computing by expanding Azure and its subscription-based services. He also made strategic acquisitions, including LinkedIn, GitHub, and Minecraft, while investing billions into artificial intelligence before it became a household name. In fact, you could say that Nadella was instrumental in Microsoft's partnership with OpenAI, as he even personally stepped in to serve as mediator when OpenAI's board briefly fired its CEO and co-founder, Sam Altman, in the fall of 2023. Although Microsoft and OpenAI renegotiated their once-exclusive partnership, Microsoft hasn't lost momentum. Their newest agreement, announced in April 2026, gave each greater independence and allowed Microsoft to continue to expand its own AI capabilities through Azure's cloud services. MSFT crossed the trillion-dollar valuation threshold on April 25, 2019, and it hasn't looked back since. In its most recent earnings, the company reported that Azure revenue grew by 43% year-over-year. These results show that Microsoft isn't just one of the founders of the digital era — it's very much a power player, and as the driver behind its innovation, Nadella himself has been rewarded handsomely through salary increases, bonuses, and enormous stock awards. As of Microsoft's latest Proxy statement for fiscal 2025, filed in September 2025, Satya Nadella owned 900,572 shares of Microsoft, equating to about 0.01% of the company's total outstanding shares. Given MSFT's October 19 closing share price of $533.52, those shares would be worth a whopping $480.4 million. But Nadella isn't Microsoft's biggest individual shareholder — not by a long shot. That distinction actually belongs to Steve Ballmer, who is estimated to still own approximately 319 million shares, or roughly 4% of Microsoft. Despite Ballmer stepping down amid Microsoft's struggles, he still owns more than 350 times as much as Nadella's stake. And in case you're wondering, even Microsoft's founder Bill Gates still owns about 103 million shares, valued at approximately $43 billion. That's substantially more than Nadella — even though Gates has spent decades giving away his fortune. Related: How much MSFT stock does Microsoft founder Bill Gates actually own? To say that Microsoft's board of directors has been happy with Nadella's efforts is an understatement. In the company's latest Proxy statement, published in October 2025, the board stated that "Our exceptional fiscal year 2025 results demonstrate that Satya Nadella and his leadership team have positioned Microsoft as a clear artificial intelligence leader for this generational technology shift, enabling Microsoft to drive long-term growth through innovation, security, and quality." Crediting Nadella for the company's 15% annual revenue growth and 17% increase in operating income, the esteemed CEO received a 117.00% payout in annual cash incentives and a 103.69% payout in performance stock awards. Translated into dollars and cents, Nadella compensation can be broken down as follows: In total, approximately 87% of Nadella's compensation was in stock awards. The $96.5 million compensation Nadella received in fiscal 2025 was an increase of about 22% from fiscal 2024, when he made $79.1 million.
